why_correct: Idealism holds that reality is ultimately spiritual and that the individual is part of a universal mind or spirit. On that view the child is an integral part of the ultimate universe, and education draws out the spiritual self already present.

why_wrong.0: Realism holds that the material world exists independently of the mind, and treats the child as one object among others in it.
why_wrong.1: Pragmatism judges ideas by their practical consequences and sees no fixed ultimate reality to be part of.
why_wrong.2: Existentialism begins from the individual's own freedom and choice, and resists absorbing the person into any larger whole.

why_correct: Rabindranath Tagore taught that education must take place in communion with nature. At Santiniketan classes were held in the open air under the trees, because he believed a child shut indoors is cut off from the source of learning.

why_wrong.0: Vivekananda's emphasis was on man-making education and the manifestation of inner perfection.
why_wrong.1: Sri Aurobindo taught integral education, aiming at the full development of the physical, vital, mental and spiritual being.
why_wrong.3: Gandhi's Basic Education centred on a productive craft and the mother tongue. All four are Indian educationists, so the phrase itself is the clue.

why_correct: Naturalism advocates discipline by natural or direct consequences, an idea from Rousseau. A child who breaks a window and must sit in the cold learns from the consequence itself rather than from punishment.

why_wrong.0: Existentialism emphasises self-chosen responsibility rather than a scheme of consequences.
why_wrong.1: Pragmatism favours social discipline, learnt through group activity and shared purpose.
why_wrong.3: Realism favours discipline through training and habit formation. Each philosophy has its own view of discipline, and natural consequences belong to the naturalists.

why_correct: Epistemology is the theory of knowledge, dealing with what knowledge is, where it comes from and how it is validated. A teacher whose business is to promote knowledge is therefore directly concerned with it.

why_wrong.0: Values are the province of axiology, which shapes the aims of education rather than its content.
why_wrong.1: Truth is close, and epistemology certainly examines it, but the teacher's day-to-day aim is stated as promoting knowledge, which is the wider term.
why_wrong.3: Skills matter in teaching, but the branch of philosophy that studies them is not epistemology in the first instance.

why_correct: Caste is named the major constraint on social change in India because it is a hereditary structure that fixes status, occupation and marriage from birth, and it resists change from within rather than merely slowing it.

why_wrong.1: Education is an agent of social change rather than a constraint on it, which makes it the odd one out here.
why_wrong.2: Religion can obstruct change where it sanctions custom, so it is a genuine constraint. But religious belief itself has also driven reform, from Buddha to the Brahmo Samaj, so its effect runs both ways.
why_wrong.3: Poverty is a real barrier too, and it keeps people from schooling and mobility. It is, however, a condition that change aims to remove, whereas caste is the structure that has most persistently resisted removal.

why_correct: Buddhist education admitted students by interest and aptitude rather than by birth, opening the monasteries to all castes. That openness is one of the ways Buddhism broke with the Vedic order.

why_wrong.0: Islamic education was organised in maktabs and madrasas around religious instruction.
why_wrong.1: Vedic education restricted study of the Vedas by caste, with the upper varnas alone admitted.
why_wrong.3: Jainistic education was also open in spirit, but the phrase and the practice described here belong to the Buddhist system, with its great universities at Nalanda and Taxila.

why_correct: Albert Bandura's social learning theory is also called observational learning or modelling. His Bobo doll experiment showed that children copy behaviour they have merely watched, without being rewarded for it themselves.

why_wrong.0: Insight learning is Kohler's, demonstrated with chimpanzees who solved a problem suddenly rather than by trial and error.
why_wrong.2: Sign learning is Tolman's theory, in which the learner builds a cognitive map of signs leading to goals.
why_wrong.3: Verbal learning concerns the acquisition of words and associations, studied by Ebbinghaus among others.

why_correct: Pragmatism judges education by its usefulness in life, so it favours a vocational and activity-based curriculum. Learning by doing is its central method, and Dewey is its leading figure.

why_wrong.0: Realism emphasises scientific knowledge and the study of the material world.
why_wrong.1: Naturalism emphasises free growth according to the child's own nature, without imposed ends.
why_wrong.3: Idealism emphasises the humanities, moral and spiritual values, and would regard a purely vocational aim as too narrow.

why_correct: The aim of idealistic education is self-realisation, that is the full unfolding of the spiritual self and its union with the ultimate reality. All other aims are subordinate to it.

why_wrong.1: Physical development is stressed by naturalism, which begins from the body and the senses.
why_wrong.2: Intuition is valued in idealism, but as a means of apprehending reality rather than as the aim.
why_wrong.3: Practical usefulness is the pragmatist aim, and idealism is often criticised for neglecting it.

why_correct: Swami Vivekananda defined education as the manifestation of the perfection already existing in man. The teacher does not add anything but removes what obstructs, as a gardener does not make the plant grow but removes the weeds.

why_wrong.0: Gandhi defined education as an all-round drawing out of the best in child and man, in body, mind and spirit.
why_wrong.2: Tagore stressed harmony with nature and freedom of the creative spirit.
why_wrong.3: Sri Aurobindo taught integral education towards a higher consciousness. All four are close in spirit, so the exact wording must be matched to its author.

why_correct: Epistemology is the branch of philosophy dealing with the nature, sources and validity of knowledge. It asks what we can know and how we come to know it.

why_wrong.1: Metaphysics deals with the nature of ultimate reality, asking what exists rather than how we know it.
why_wrong.2: Logic deals with the principles of valid reasoning and correct inference.
why_wrong.3: Ethics deals with right and wrong conduct, and belongs with aesthetics under axiology.

why_correct: John Locke denied innate ideas in his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, arguing that all knowledge comes from experience through sensation and reflection. He is the founder of British empiricism.

why_wrong.1: David Hume was an empiricist too and pushed the position further into scepticism, but the explicit attack on innate ideas is Locke's.
why_wrong.2: Descartes maintained the opposite, holding that certain ideas such as God and extension are innate.
why_wrong.3: Leibniz also defended innate ideas, replying directly to Locke in his New Essays. The rationalists affirm innate ideas and the empiricists deny them, and that is the divide being tested.

why_correct: John Locke described the mind at birth as a tabula rasa, a blank slate on which experience writes. It is the same doctrine as the denial of innate ideas, stated as an image.

why_wrong.0: Bishop Berkeley held that to be is to be perceived, a form of subjective idealism.
why_wrong.2: Hume analysed the mind into impressions and ideas and denied a permanent self, which is a further step rather than this one.
why_wrong.3: John Stuart Mill was a utilitarian and a logician of the following century.

why_correct: Descartes took mathematics as the model of certain knowledge, because its truths are clear, distinct and independent of the senses. He built his whole method on that ideal.

why_wrong.0: Christian Wolff systematised Leibniz's philosophy but is not the source of this claim.
why_wrong.1: Spinoza wrote his Ethics in geometrical form, so he certainly admired mathematical method, but the doctrine is credited to Descartes.
why_wrong.3: Leibniz was a great mathematician and co-inventor of the calculus, yet the statement belongs to Descartes.

why_correct: The playground is an informal agency of education. There is no syllabus and no teacher, yet a child learns cooperation, fair play, leadership and how to lose, simply by playing.

why_wrong.1: A library is part of the formal system, organised deliberately to support study.
why_wrong.2: A seminar is a planned academic meeting, so it is formal.
why_wrong.3: A classroom is the most formal agency of all. The test is whether the learning is planned and deliberate, and only the playground's is not.

why_correct: Charvaka is materialist and holds that man is nothing but the physical body, formed from the four elements. Consciousness arises from that combination and ends with it, so there is no soul surviving death.

why_wrong.1: A self distinct from the body is what Charvaka expressly denies.
why_wrong.2: Consciousness for Charvaka is a property that emerges from matter, like the intoxicating power that arises when ingredients ferment, not an independent reality.
why_wrong.3: Charvaka has a definite answer here, so none of these is wrong.

why_correct: Charvaka accepts perception alone as a valid means of knowledge and rejects both inference and testimony, because neither can be verified by the senses. That is what makes it the most radical of the Indian schools.

why_wrong.0: Inference is rejected, but so is testimony, so naming only one is incomplete.
why_wrong.1: Testimony is rejected as well, and for the same reason.
why_wrong.3: Charvaka certainly challenges both. Its whole epistemology reduces to pratyaksha, direct perception, which is why it can deny the soul, God and life after death.

why_correct: Liberation in Buddhism is nirvana, the extinction of craving and thereby of suffering and rebirth. The word literally means blowing out, as of a flame.

why_wrong.1: Moksha is the term used in Hindu philosophy for release from the cycle of birth and death.
why_wrong.2: Mukti is another Hindu term for the same release, used interchangeably with moksha.
why_wrong.3: There is a proper term, so none of these is wrong. Each tradition has its own word, and matching word to tradition is what the question tests.

why_correct: Jainism prescribes all three. Penance burns away accumulated karma, self-control prevents new karma from binding, and detachment from possessions and passions frees the soul. Together they lead to liberation.

why_wrong.0: Penance, or tapas, is essential in Jainism but is only one part of the path.
why_wrong.1: Self-control through the vows is likewise necessary but not sufficient by itself.
why_wrong.2: Detachment, aparigraha, is the third element. Since each is genuinely required, all of these is the answer, and the path is often summed up as the Three Jewels of right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.

why_correct: Charvaka neglects liberation altogether. Being materialist, it denies the soul and rebirth, so there is nothing to be liberated and nothing to be liberated from. Its aim is pleasure in this life.

why_wrong.1: Jainism makes liberation central, achieved by shedding karma until the soul rises to the top of the universe.
why_wrong.2: Buddhism makes nirvana its whole purpose, set out in the Four Noble Truths.
why_wrong.3: Vedanta makes moksha the highest of the four ends of life. Charvaka is the one Indian school that rejects the framework entirely, which is why it is called nastika in the strongest sense.

why_correct: Swami Vivekananda held that all knowledge, material and spiritual, is already within us and is merely veiled by ignorance. It follows that education uncovers rather than supplies.

why_wrong.0: Tagore's emphasis was on freedom, nature and creative expression.
why_wrong.2: Gandhi's emphasis was on craft, character and self-reliance.
why_wrong.3: Plato held that learning is recollection of what the soul knew before birth, which is a genuinely similar doctrine from another tradition. The Indian phrasing about the curtain of ignorance is Vivekananda's.

why_correct: Rabindranath Tagore founded Santiniketan, beginning with a school in 1901 that grew into Visva-Bharati University in 1921. Teaching there was done in the open air, in close contact with nature.

why_wrong.2: Gandhi founded Sabarmati and Sevagram ashrams and the scheme of Basic Education.
why_wrong.3: Sri Aurobindo founded the ashram at Pondicherry and its Centre of Education.

why_correct: The Vedic view is that creation is without beginning and without end, an eternal cycle of creation, preservation and dissolution repeating without a first moment or a last.

why_wrong.0: Without beginning is only half the doctrine, and leaving out the second half changes the meaning.
why_wrong.1: Without an end is the other half, and it is equally incomplete on its own.
why_wrong.3: Creation at a particular moment is the view of the Semitic traditions, and it is precisely what the cyclical Vedic conception denies.
